# Decoding Fault Code 15 on a 2002 Yamaha YZF-R1: Beyond Basic Resistance Checks

When you encounter fault code 15 on a 2002 Yamaha YZF-R1, the diagnostic process often stalls after verifying the most obvious electrical parameters. You have likely already confirmed that the Throttle Position Sensor (TPS) exhibits correct resistance across all cable combinations. You've verified the yellow-black wire shows the expected voltage when the ignition is active and disconnected from the harness. Furthermore, you have measured continuity between the wire harness connector and the ECU connector, ruling out broken cables in the main harness.

If your multimeter reads perfect values but the ECU continues to log fault code 15, you are facing a classic "good signal, bad interpretation" scenario. The issue is rarely that a component has failed electrically; it is usually that the system's logic thresholds or synchronization are not aligning with what the ECU expects. In automotive diagnostics, measuring static resistance and voltage only tells half the story. The other half lies in dynamic behavior and signal integrity within the context of the Engine Control Unit (ECU).

The TPS on a 2002 R1 is not just a resistor; it is a potentiometer that generates an analog voltage curve mapped to specific throttle angles. While static resistance checks confirm the internal coil isn't open or shorted, they do not validate the *linearity* of the output. The ECU expects a precise voltage ramp as you twist the grip. If the TPS signal jumps, lags, or deviates slightly from the factory mapâeven if the endpoints are within specâthe ECU will flag a fault. A common pitfall is checking resistance with the throttle closed and open but neglecting the mid-range sweep. The ECU might be rejecting a value of 2.3V at 50% throttle because it expects 2.31V, based on its internal calibration table.

Another critical area to investigate is the ground reference for the TPS signal circuit. You checked the yellow-black wire's voltage relative to the battery or ignition supply, but have you verified the stability of the ECU ground? A high-resistance ground path between the sensor connector and the chassis can introduce noise or slight voltage drops under load, causing the ECU to misinterpret a healthy signal as an anomaly. Use an oscilloscope if possible to check for ripple or noise on the TPS line while the engine is idling. Static DC measurements often mask AC interference that triggers intermittent fault codes.

Furthermore, consider the mechanical alignment of the throttle body itself. On this generation of YZF-R1, the throttle bodies are electronically controlled and must be synchronized when reassembled after a maintenance interval. If the throttle plates were not perfectly aligned with the ECU's learned base position, the TPS reading will never match the actuator's physical state, leading to a persistent fault code regardless of electrical continuity. The ECU compares the mechanical angle derived from the stepper motor commands against the actual voltage returned by the TPS. A mismatch triggers the logic error flagged as code 15.

It is also worth noting that aftermarket wiring modifications or non-OEM sensors can introduce subtle resistance changes in the connector shell or pin tension issues. Even if continuity exists, a loose mating surface can create intermittent contact that mimics a sensor failure. Ensure the TPS connector is fully seated and that the pins are not corroded inside the plastic housing.

If all physical checks pass and the wiring diagram aligns with reality, the fault may lie within the ECU's internal analog-to-digital converter (ADC) or its lookup table memory corruption. At this stage, swapping the ECU with a known-good unit from another donor bike is often more cost-effective than attempting to reflash or repair the original unit. The software logic inside the ECU determines what constitutes a "valid" signal; if that logic is compromised, no amount of perfect wiring will clear the code.
